# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of ischemic stroke, accounting for substantial morbidity and mortality worldwide [1]. Oral anticoagulation (OAC) with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) remains the cornerstone of stroke prevention in patients with AF [2]. However, a considerable proportion of patients have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation or experience major bleeding [3]. Because the left atrial appendage (LAA) is the source of more than 90% of thrombi in non-valvular AF, percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) has emerged as a mechanical alternative for stroke prevention [4,5].

## Rationale and Anatomy

The LAA is a remnant of the embryonic left atrium with a highly variable trabeculated morphology, often classified as "chicken wing," "windsock," "cactus," or "cauliflower" types [6]. Stasis within the appendage during AF promotes thrombus formation, providing the anatomical and pathophysiological basis for device-based exclusion [4]. Accurate preprocedural imaging with transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) or cardiac computed tomography is essential for sizing and procedural planning [7].

## Devices and Technique

Two principal endocardial devices dominate contemporary practice. The Watchman device (Boston Scientific) was the first to undergo rigorous randomized evaluation, while the Amplatzer Amulet (Abbott) employs a dual-seal "lobe-and-disc" design [8,9]. The procedure is performed via transseptal puncture under fluoroscopic and echocardiographic guidance, with intracardiac echocardiography increasingly used as an alternative to TEE [10]. Epicardial approaches such as the LARIAT suture-ligation system offer an alternative for patients with absolute anticoagulation contraindications [11].

## Evidence from Randomized Trials

The pivotal PROTECT AF trial demonstrated that Watchman closure was non-inferior to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death in non-valvular AF [8]. Longer-term follow-up confirmed durable benefits, with reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and cardiovascular mortality [12]. The subsequent PREVAIL trial addressed early procedural safety concerns and, combined with PROTECT AF in a patient-level meta-analysis, supported the efficacy of LAAC, particularly in reducing disabling stroke and bleeding [13,14]. The PRAGUE-17 trial compared LAAC with DOACs in high-risk patients and found non-inferiority for major cardiovascular and bleeding events [15]. The Amulet IDE trial established non-inferiority of the Amulet device versus Watchman, with the dual-seal device achieving higher rates of complete closure [9].

## Registries and Real-World Outcomes

Large registries have complemented trial data. The EWOLUTION registry demonstrated high implantation success and low rates of device-related thrombus and stroke in a population largely ineligible for OAC [16]. The National Cardiovascular Data Registry LAAO Registry, encompassing tens of thousands of US procedures, reported high procedural success with acceptable complication rates in routine practice [17]. Analyses of the Amulet device in observational cohorts have similarly shown favorable outcomes [18].

## Procedural Complications and Device-Related Thrombus

Complications include pericardial effusion and tamponade, device embolization, and vascular access events; periprocedural risk has declined with operator experience and improved imaging [19,20]. Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in approximately 2–4% of patients and is associated with increased thromboembolic risk [21,22]. Incomplete closure with peridevice leaks remains a concern, although the clinical significance of small leaks is debated [23,24]. Optimal post-procedural antithrombotic regimens—ranging from dual antiplatelet therapy to short-course DOAC—continue to be refined [25].

## Guidelines and Patient Selection

Current guidelines assign LAAC a role primarily in patients with high stroke risk and contraindications to long-term anticoagulation, reflecting a Class IIb recommendation in many societies [2,26]. Appropriate patient selection, shared decision-making, and a multidisciplinary heart-team approach are emphasized [27]. Ongoing trials such as CHAMPION-AF and OPTION are evaluating LAAC as a first-line alternative to OAC in broader populations, which may expand indications [28].

## Future Directions

Refinements in device technology, including improved sealing and biocompatibility, aim to reduce DRT and residual leaks [29]. Combining LAAC with other structural interventions and advances in imaging-guided procedural planning are areas of active investigation [30]. As randomized data accumulate comparing LAAC with contemporary DOAC therapy, the role of mechanical appendage exclusion in mainstream stroke prevention will become clearer.

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC is an established option for stroke prevention in selected AF patients, particularly those unsuitable for long-term anticoagulation. Robust trial and registry data support its safety and efficacy, but questions regarding optimal antithrombotic management, DRT, and expanded indications remain. Continued randomized investigation will determine whether LAAC can be positioned as a broader alternative to pharmacological therapy.
